Snippet-only first-party numbers cap at C, matching wave 10 precedents (font-rs, blaze).

corrections.baseline: ImageMagick's built-in colour quantization (an old ImageMagick 6-era version, not stated); no pngnq, Pillow quantize or other baseline numbers were found in the repo
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search-result text, page blocked): a fast-and-rough speed setting 'that is 2.5 to 6 times faster than ImageMagick's current algorithm while still mostly winning in quality'. The search engine attributes this to the 'Use pngquant (libimagequant) for quantization to palette' thread on the legacy ImageMagick forum, the author's proposal to adopt libimagequant in ImageMagick, not to pngquant.org (a site:pngquant.org search returned no ImageMagick comparison). The second figure is a self-comparison from the man page pngquant.1: 'Speed 10 has 5% lower quality, but is about 8 times faster than the default' (the man page says the default is 3; the current CLI help in pngquant.c and the README say the default is 4).
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the ImageMagick ratio lives in a blocked, old forum thread written by the author, with no images, settings, versions or hardware visible, and it compares a fast-and-rough pngquant setting against ImageMagick's default quantizer, so speed and quality settings differ (different work: pngquant's adaptive dithering and perceptual quality model vs ImageMagick's own quantizer and dithering). The 8x figure compares pngquant against itself. pngquant 3 replaced the C libimagequant with the Rust imagequant crate (CHANGELOG 3.0), so the quantization engine is Rust and only the CLI is C. Dual-licensed GPL-3.0-or-later or commercial (Super Source); the GPL option makes it copyable but copyleft.

notes: Speed claim is against ImageMagick's quantizer, not pngnq or Pillow; the record's source attribution (pngquant.org) looks wrong, the text comes from the ImageMagick forum thread t=23340 per search results, which I could not open (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so it is not in urls_opened. tier_reason: First-party page with public harness (test/bench/perf.js, test/bench/Dockerfile, test/bench/run-with-docker.sh, test/bench/package.json) and stated CPUs (AWS c8a.xlarge, 4x AMD EPYC 9R45; c8g.xlarge, 4x Graviton4), but no compiler version or flags: the addon is built from source with an unstated Ubuntu 25.10 gcc, libvips is a prebuilt binary, and ImageMagick/GraphicsMagick are unversioned distribution packages. Code plus CPU without compiler/flags is C, the same tier the libvips record got in batch-05.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. test/bench/Dockerfile (Ubuntu 25.10, build-essential, Node.js 24 via nodesource) runs npm install, npm run build:dist and npm run build, so the sharp addon is compiled from source with node-gyp (src/binding.gyp adds -flto=auto on glibc) against the prebuilt @img/sharp-libvips libvips; gcc version not stated. Page versions: sharp v0.35.0, libvips v8.18.2 with libvips caching disabled (sharp.cache(false)), Node.js 24.15.0, sharp.concurrency set to the physical core count. ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick are Ubuntu 25.10 apt packages, versions not stated.
corrections.baseline: ImageMagick convert CLI through the npm 'imagemagick' v0.1.3 wrapper and GraphicsMagick gm CLI through npm 'gm' v1.25.1 (Ubuntu 25.10 packages, versions not stated); jimp v1.6.1 (pure JavaScript) is also on the page
corrections.claimed_speedup: JPEG AMD64: sharp 88.21 ops/s (file), 89.63 (buffer), 82.87 (stream) vs imagemagick 16.23 (file) and gm 21.04 (file), 20.92 (buffer): 5.43x vs ImageMagick and 4.19x vs gm file-to-file (derived from page data). JPEG ARM64: sharp 52.42 (file) vs imagemagick 5.85 and gm 13.72: 8.96x and 3.82x (derived from page data). PNG AMD64: sharp 47.17 (file) vs imagemagick 10.37 and gm 13.35: 4.55x and 3.53x (derived from page data; page speed-up column 4.5 vs 1.0). PNG ARM64: sharp 28.04 vs imagemagick 4.39 and gm 9.45: 6.39x and 2.97x (derived from page data). README: 'typically 4x-5x faster than using the quickest ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick settings'.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. The JPEG task is not the same work for each contender: sharp's default fastShrinkOnLoad makes libjpeg decode the 2725x2225 input at 1/2 scale (the 3.78x reduction selects shrink 2 in src/pipeline.cc) before Lanczos3, while the npm imagemagick wrapper runs 'convert in -set option:filter:blur 0.8 -filter Lanczos -strip -resize 720x588 -quality 80 out' with no jpeg:size hint, so ImageMagick decodes the full image (and uses a sharpened Lanczos); gm is called without a size hint too. The PNG task has no shrink-on-load and is closer to like-for-like. ImageMagick and gm are spawned as a new process per image, adding start-up and file I/O; the page calls the imagemagick wrapper unmaintained and gm sunset. libvips caching is disabled. sharp is a Node.js native wrapper over libvips, so the speed is libvips's; compare the libvips entry in this wave.

notes: Numbers all match docs/src/content/docs/performance.md. sharp is a Node.js wrapper over libvips (already recorded this wave, tier C), so the orchestrator may want decision duplicate; its bench does compare against ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick (and jimp) with stated EC2 machines. tier_reason: First-party criterion tables in README.md with public harness (app/benches/yuv8/main.rs, app/Cargo.toml) and bench commands, but no Rust toolchain version, no libyuv commit, and CPU models only for the M3 and i9-14900HX columns (m4.large and c5.large CPUs unstated), so not A; no independent measurement, so not B. Tier stays C; verdict is downgrade because the headline 2.3x NV12 ratio is not like-for-like.

corrections.baseline: libyuv built from source by the yuv-sys 0.3.x crate (livekit/rust-sdks, required as 0.3.7 in app/Cargo.toml); libyuv commit not stated
corrections.claimed_speedup: README says performance is 'equal to libyuv or slightly higher on platforms where SIMD is implemented. Otherwise, equal or slower.' The record's headline NEON 'NV12 to RGB 273.38 us vs libyuv 621.11 us' (2.27x) is not like-for-like: in app/benches/yuv8/main.rs the libyuv row calls rs_NV21ToABGR into a 4-byte-per-pixel buffer while the yuvutils row writes 3-byte RGB. Like-for-like rows (derived from page data): NV12 to RGBA 377.59 vs 621.11 us on NEON (1.64x), 917.52 us vs 979.96 us on AVX2 (1.07x), 736.21 vs 800.85 us on AVX-512 (1.09x); YUV 4:2:0 to RGB 346.13 vs 675.72 us NEON (1.95x), 923.83 us vs 1.42 ms AVX2 (1.54x), 614.19 us vs 1.16 ms AVX-512 (1.89x); YUV 4:2:0 to RGBA 396.58 vs 710.88 us NEON (1.79x), 942.92 us vs 1.03 ms AVX2 (1.09x), 733.88 vs 870.64 us AVX-512 (1.19x); RGB to YUV 4:2:0 255.25 vs 306.80 us NEON (1.20x), 973.17 us vs 1.10 ms AVX2 (1.13x), 722.87 vs 972.52 us AVX-512 (1.35x).
corrections.hardware: README: 'Mac Pro M3' (aarch64, NEON); AWS m4.large with Ubuntu 24.04 (AVX2, CPU model not stated); Windows 11 Intel Core i9-14900HX (AVX2); AWS c5.large with Ubuntu 24.04 (AVX-512, CPU model not stated); 1997x1331 test image (assets/bench.jpg)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench yuv8 --manifest-path ./app/Cargo.toml --features fast_mode,professional_mode,rdm (AVX-512: cargo +nightly bench ... --features nightly_avx512,fast_mode,professional_mode); criterion 0.6, sample size 500, 7 s measurement time; Rust toolchain version not stated (app/Cargo.toml also enables the yuv crate's nightly_i8mm and nightly_f16 features); libyuv compiled by the yuv-sys build script through the cc crate, flags not stated
corrections.caveats: libyuv wins several rows: YUV 4:0:0 to RGBA on AVX2 (635.61 vs 651.88 us) and AVX-512 (525.56 vs 600.43 us), YUV 4:4:4 to RGBA on AVX2 (963.66 us vs 1.10 ms) and AVX-512 (803.62 vs 819.17 us), YUV 4:2:2 to RGBA on AVX2 (1.04 vs 1.10 ms), RGBA to YUV 4:2:0 and 4:2:2 on AVX-512, and 10-bit to RGBA8 on AVX2. The Windows AVX2 column has libyuv at 2.70-6.86 ms on the encode, RGB24-output and 10-bit rows but 525.90-579.24 us on 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 to RGBA, consistent with a libyuv build (likely MSVC) missing some SIMD row paths (inference, not stated), so the 7-16x gaps on those rows should be ignored. The README rows do not say which YuvConversionMode (Fast, Balanced, Professional) was timed; Fast is documented as libyuv-level precision, Balanced as more precise and about 30% slower. The libyuv 4:2:2 encode row uses ABGRToJ422 (full range) against yuvutils limited range. SIMD and scalar yuvutils paths disagree by up to 2 levels on x86 (issue #144, open, opened 2026-10-02); bit-exactness against libyuv was not shown either way.

notes: Rust crate (yuv on crates.io, 4.27M downloads), language-filter mismatch for a C++-first catalog; language field Rust is already right. Every number in the record is in README.md, but the NV12 headline compares 3-byte RGB output with libyuv's 4-byte ABGR (NV21) call, so the real lead is 1.1-1.6x on NV12 and 1.1-2x elsewhere, with libyuv ahead on several x86 rows.
